slides.title: Lists

blocks.text: A list is a linear collection whose elements can be added and removed in a flexible way.
Unlike a stack or queue, an element can be added or removed anywhere in a list.

slides.title: Three Types of List Collections

blocks.text: Ordered Lists
The elements are always ordered as they are added into the list
For examples, a list of people ordered alphabetically by name
The list is always sorted based on some key value
Unordered Lists
The elements have no inherent order and are not sorted
A new element can be put at the front, rear, or anywhere in the list
Indexed Lists
The elements can be referenced using a numeric index

slides.title: Using Lists: Program of Study

blocks.text: The ProgramOfStudy class stores a list of Course objects.
It uses an indexed list to manage the courses that a student takes to fulfill the degree requirements.
The Course class represents a course, which may or may not have already been taken.
We will use the ArrayList class from the Java collections
API to manage the list of courses.
We will write a POSTester class to create a new program of study and test the ProgramOfStudy class.

slides.title: Array Implementation of a List

blocks.text: An indexed list can be implemented easily using an array.
The list keeps track of the count of elements.
The list elements are indexed from 0 to count – 1.
Since the elements can be added and removed at any index, shifting the elements in the array is necessary.

slides.title: Implementing a List with Links

blocks.text: We can implement an indexed list collection as a singly linked list of Node objects, as we did with queues.
We can efficiently remove a node at the front of the list.
However, we cannot efficiently remove a node at the rear of middle of the singly linked list.
Singly Linked List
An integer count keeps track of the size of the list.

slides.title: Doubly Linked List

blocks.text: We need a doubly linked list to efficiently remove any node.
Each node in a doubly linked list stores references to the previous node before it and the next node after it.
A doubly linked list can be traversed forward and backward.
Insertions and deletions can be done efficiently at arbitrary positions.

slides.title: Removing a Node from Doubly Linked List

blocks.text: Removing the front node is very simple and done in few steps.
Removing a node at an index requires traversing the linked list. The node at index–1 is relinked to the successor node at index+1.
Removing the first occurrence of an element requires searching the linked list locating the first node that has the target element. The previous node is then relinked to the successor node.
